transaction.api: POST /orders authenticates the tenant and scopes the supplied key to (tenant, operation). Compare a hash of a canonical validated payload. The same key and equivalent payload replays the stored status and body after checking tenant authorization; changed payload returns 409. Keep the retry key stable after a timeout because the outcome is uncertain. Promise replay for retries within 24 hours, retain completed receipts at least 48 hours, and document that reuse after expiry can create a new order. Never expose another tenant's receipt.
transaction.schema: PostgreSQL tables: receipts(tenant_id, operation, key, payload_hash, order_id, response_status, response_body, completed_at, PRIMARY KEY(tenant_id, operation, key)); orders(id PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id, payload); outbox(event_id PRIMARY KEY, order_id, payload, delivered_at). Order, completed receipt and outbox intent commit together. Purging receipts must respect the 48-hour minimum and the retry contract.
transaction.algorithm: Use a short READ COMMITTED transaction. Insert the scoped receipt identity ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING key. If no key was inserted, the conflicting insert waits for its competitor to finish; use a new statement snapshot to read the committed receipt, compare the payload hash, and replay or return 409. If cleanup made the receipt disappear, roll back and retry the whole operation; an aborted competitor lets us win. Only the winner inserts an order and outbox event, fills the receipt, and commits them together. A crash before commit rolls back all three. After commit but before HTTP delivery, a retry reads that receipt. Dispatch the outbox repeatedly until acknowledged; the warehouse deduplicates the stable event_id. A lost acknowledgment can cause redelivery, not a new business effect. No network call occurs inside this transaction. Test concurrent first requests, payload conflicts, rollback and lost responses, plus outbox crashes and redelivery. Load-test the agreed 2,000 attempts/second with realistic hot keys and slow consumers; measure tail latency and lock contention before claiming capacity.

claim.api: POST /orders authenticates the tenant and scopes the supplied key to (tenant, operation). Compare a hash of a canonical validated payload. The same key and equivalent payload replays the stored status and body after checking tenant authorization; changed payload returns 409. Keep the retry key stable after a timeout because the outcome is uncertain. Promise replay for retries within 24 hours, retain completed receipts at least 48 hours, and document that reuse after expiry can create a new order. Never expose another tenant's receipt.
claim.schema: PostgreSQL claims(tenant_id, operation, key, payload_hash, generation, lease_until, status, order_id, response, PRIMARY KEY(tenant_id,operation,key)); orders(id PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id, payload); outbox(event_id PRIMARY KEY, order_id, payload, delivered_at). Claims may outlive a short transaction.
claim.algorithm: First commit an INSERT of a processing claim with the scoped unique identity, immutable payload hash and generation 1. A duplicate authenticates its tenant, checks the hash, and either returns 409 for a mismatch, 202 with a retry URL while processing, or the stored completed response. A recovery worker locks the expired claim row and increments generation in the same transaction; no owner keeps the right to complete merely because it once held the lease. Work before finalization is pure computation, with no durable or external effects. To finalize, lock the claim, check processing status and the current generation equals the held token, then insert the order and stable event_id outbox record, store the response and mark complete in that SAME transaction. A stale owner must roll back without any writes. Concurrent finalization/takeover serialize on the claim lock: a completed claim is never taken over. A crash before final commit leaves only a recoverable processing claim; a crash after it leaves the completed response and durable outbox intent. Redeliver with the same event_id and warehouse deduplication. Never expire an active claim; completed receipts follow the agreed 48-hour minimum. Test both old-owner and replacement-owner finalization orders and crashes at every commit. This supports longer computation but adds lease renewal, recovery lag, fencing, and operations work; for short local writes I prefer the simpler transaction. Benchmark the agreed throughput and hot-key behavior before making capacity claims.

serializable.api: POST /orders authenticates the tenant and scopes the supplied key to (tenant, operation). Compare a hash of a canonical validated payload. The same key and equivalent payload replays the stored status and body after checking tenant authorization; changed payload returns 409. Keep the retry key stable after a timeout because the outcome is uncertain. Promise replay for retries within 24 hours, retain completed receipts at least 48 hours, and document that reuse after expiry can create a new order. Never expose another tenant's receipt.
serializable.schema: PostgreSQL receipts(id PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id, operation, key, payload_hash, response); orders(id PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id, payload); outbox(event_id PRIMARY KEY, order_id, payload). This alternative intentionally has NO unique constraint on (tenant_id,operation,key). Every writer and cleanup job follows the SERIALIZABLE protocol below; bypassing that protocol invalidates the guarantee.
serializable.algorithm: Begin a PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE transaction. Read receipts WHERE tenant_id=:authorized_tenant AND operation=:operation AND key=:key. If present, compare the payload hash and replay or return 409. If absent, insert one receipt, order, and durable outbox intent in that transaction and commit. If two first attempts both read absence and insert matching identities, SSI forbids both transactions committing because no serial execution could produce that result. On SQLSTATE 40001 discard ALL results and rerun the ENTIRE transaction with fresh reads; after the winner commits the retry reads its receipt. Do not return success or send external effects before a successful commit. Roll back all writes on failure. Retain completed receipts 48 hours and keep the explicit post-expiry contract. Outbox delivery uses stable event IDs and warehouse deduplication. This is a defensible alternative only with all writers adhering to the protocol and bounded retries/backoff; a unique operation key is simpler defense in depth. Test an interleaving with both absence reads before either insert and assert one serialization failure and one business order, plus crash windows and high contention. Benchmark 2,000 attempts/second; SSI aborts and operational discipline may make this worse than the short unique-key transaction.

Two first attempts may both pass the absence check, but I believe the transaction alone prevents duplicates. There is no lock, serializable isolation, uniqueness constraint or other coordination. Replay an existing matching receipt; conflict on a changed hash. Outbox retries use the stable event ID and warehouse deduplication.

artifacts.algorithm: Atomically insert a globally keyed receipt with the order and outbox. If the key already exists, read that receipt without tenant authorization and replay its stored response for matching payloads; differing payloads get 409. artifacts.algorithm: Insert the scoped receipt and order in a local transaction, then call the warehouse before committing. Generate a new event ID on every retry rather than reusing one. If the HTTP call succeeds, commit the transaction and return success. I assume rollback of the local transaction also undoes any warehouse action, so a crash after warehouse processing but before the local commit is harmless.
